headline: The drug was
body: Given for an unrelated tumour. It blocks FGFR signalling broadly instead of targeting one receptor. The skeletal overgrowth was a side effect, not the point.
punch: Nobody was trying to make this kid taller.

headline: To see why that matters
body: It's caused by a gain of function mutation in FGFR3. The receptor is stuck partly on, and constant FGFR3 signalling suppresses chondrocyte proliferation in the growth plate.
punch: Too much FGFR3 signal means too little growth.

headline: So the case report
body: Block FGFR broadly and you get overgrowth. The mutation that overactivates FGFR3 gives you the opposite. Same axis, opposite directions.
punch: Real human evidence for the mechanism, found by accident.

headline: Which is why
body: TYRA-300 and infigratinib are purpose built selective inhibitors. Infigratinib reached a 2024 NEJM trial with a matching mouse model behind it.
punch: Both designed from scratch to hit this exact target.

headline: And the third one
body: Meclizine. Decades old, cheap, over the counter for motion sickness. It turned out to inhibit the same pathway and reached Phase 2 in Japan in kids with achondroplasia.
punch: A travel sickness pill and a bespoke oncology molecule aiming at the same receptor.

headline: Downstream
body: FGFR3's growth suppressing signal gets carried out by a transcription factor called Snail1, which makes it a candidate readout for whether any of these drugs is actually working.
punch: One marker for three different strategies.

headline: But be clear
body: These are treatments for a specific genetic skeletal dysplasia, tested in patients who have it. None of this is a height pathway for people without the mutation.
punch: Fixing a broken receptor is not the same as upgrading a working one.
